title: Given a 2D board of characters and a word, return true if the word exists in the grid by connecting horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell is used at most once.
shortTitle: Word Search — DFS on a grid with visited marking
topicTitle: Given a 2D board of characters and a word

s1_definition.profdef: For each cell matching the first letter, run a depth-first search that matches successive letters by moving to the four orthogonal neighbors, marking the current cell visited to prevent reuse within the path, and unmarking it on backtrack. Return true as soon as the full word is matched; otherwise continue from other start cells.
s1_definition.analogy: On a grid of stamped characters at National Bank of India, you trace a security phrase by stepping up, down, left, or right onto the next matching character, never stepping on the same cell twice in one trace. If you can spell the whole phrase, it exists on the grid.
s1_definition.oneliner: DFS from each matching start, mark cells visited along the path, unmark on backtrack, succeed when the word is fully matched.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** For each cell matching the first letter, run a depth-first search that matches successive letters by moving to the four orthogonal neighbors, marking the current cell visited to prevent reuse within the path, and unmarking it on backtrack. Return true as soon as the full word is matched; otherwise continue from other start cells.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** On a grid of stamped characters at National Bank of India, you trace a security phrase by stepping up, down, left, or right onto the next matching character, never stepping on the same cell twice in one trace. If you can spell the whole phrase, it exists on the grid.

**One line to remember:** DFS from each matching start, mark cells visited along the path, unmark on backtrack, succeed when the word is fully matched.

sections.s2_technical:
For each cell, call a DFS carrying the index of the next character to match. If the index equals the word length, return true. If out of bounds, mismatched, or already visited, return false. Otherwise mark the cell (for instance temporarily overwrite it), try the four directions, then restore it. For example: `char tmp = board[r][c]; board[r][c] = '#'; boolean found = dfs(...up) || ...; board[r][c] = tmp;`.

Temporarily overwriting the cell is a common trick to mark visited without a separate array, restored on backtrack so other search paths can use it. Short-circuiting with `||` returns as soon as any direction succeeds.

The time is O(rows · cols · 4^L) in the worst case where L is the word length, because each start can branch four ways per letter. A senior nuance is pruning start cells by an early frequency check: if the board lacks enough of any letter in the word, fail fast.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a grid of stamped characters encodes security phrases, and a verifier must confirm whether a given phrase can be traced through adjacent cells. This is exactly how Word Search works.

Problem 2 — A single trace may not reuse a cell, though different traces may reuse it. This is exactly why cells are marked visited along the current path and restored on backtrack.

The mini-project builds a `SecurityPhraseVerifier`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a three-by-three grid and the phrase NBIEY.

Step 1: DFS starts at (0,0) matching N, marks it, and moves right to (0,1) matching B.

Step 2: From B it moves right to (0,2) matching I, then down to (1,2) matching E, then down to (2,2) matching Y.

Step 3: The index now equals the phrase length, so the trace returns true and each visited cell is restored on the way back.

Step 4: For NBZ, no neighbor of B matches Z, so all branches fail and the verifier returns false.

```text
2026-10-27T00:30:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Security Phrase Verifier (Word Search)
2026-10-27T00:30:00Z [INFO] Phrase 'NBIEY' traced successfully
2026-10-27T00:30:00Z [INFO] NBIEY present? true
2026-10-27T00:30:00Z [WARNING] Phrase 'NBZ' not found on grid
2026-10-27T00:30:00Z [INFO] NBZ present? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  start cells matching word[0]='N' → (0,0)
    (0,0)N → (0,1)B → (0,2)I → (1,2)E → (2,2)Y → idx==len → TRUE
    mark '#' on enter, restore on exit (path-local visited)
  NBZ: B has no 'Z' neighbor → FALSE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search is grid backtracking. I scan the board for cells matching the first letter and launch a depth-first search from each, carrying the index of the next letter I need to match. The search succeeds when that index reaches the word length, and it fails when I step off the board, hit a mismatch, or revisit a cell already on the current path. For each matching cell I mark it visited, try all four orthogonal directions, and then restore it on the way back so other search paths can still use it.

A neat trick is to mark the cell by temporarily overwriting its character with a sentinel and restoring it on backtrack, which avoids a separate visited array. The short-circuit or across the four directions returns as soon as any one succeeds. The worst case is the board size times four to the word length.

In my project at National Bank of India, a grid of stamped characters encoded security phrases and a verifier confirmed whether a given phrase could be traced through adjacent cells without reusing a cell. The DFS-with-restore pattern handled it directly, and I added a quick letter-frequency pre-check so phrases requiring letters the board lacked failed fast.
